newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's Ssangyong Motor net loss soars in 1996.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's Ssangyong Motor net loss soars in 1996.

text.p: South Korean utility vehicle maker Ssangyong Motor Co on Friday said its net loss widened sharply in 1996 and disclosed steps to cut back on its increasingly heavy debt burden.

Attributing the loss to huge financial costs resulting from debts, the company said the search for more foreign investment in the firm and sales of some of its assets were core strategies to turn its results around.
"Although details have not yet been set, we plan to sell real estate, bonds and other assets to improve our financial position," Ssangyong president Lee Chong-kyu told reporters.
Ssangyong, an affiliate of the Ssangyong Group, said its after-tax net loss rose to 228.49 billion won ($260.2 million) in 1996 from a 126.23 billion won loss in 1995.
The loss was reported despite a rise in its annual turnover to 1.37 trillion won from 986.75 billion won in 1995.
"Our business performance in 1996 suffered from increased financial costs resulting from past huge capital investments," spokesman Cho Min-gyun said.
The company did not release details about its costs, however.
Ssangyong has decided to allow foreign partners to hold a stake of up to 49 percent in the company, compared with the 10 percent ceiling that applied by the end of 1996, Cho said.
"In order to reduce outside borrowing, we have no choice but to raise funds without interest. We will try to attract more foreign capital investors in that sense," Lee said.
As of the end of 1996, Germany's Daimler-Benz AG held a 2.6 percent stake in Ssangyong, which makes four-wheel drive utility vehicles and commercial vehicles.
The company's overall liabilities stood at far more than 10 times its equity capital at the end of 1996, analysts said.
Ssangyong's debt-equity ratio stood at 1,024.4 percent at the end of 1995 and 962.3 percent at end-1994.
Exact figures for 1996 were not immediately available.
Ssangyong's chronic losses have sparked recurring speculation on the local stock market that it was a target for a takeover bid by the giant Samsung Group.
The speculation has been officially denied by Ssangyong and Samsung, which itself is due to enter the already crowded car market from next year through Samsung Motors Inc.
Analysts said Ssangyong's concentration on high-priced vehicles aimed at niche markets would continue to suppress the company's earnings in the future.

"Unless it makes a big hit on the mass consumption market of cheap passenger cars, it's hard to expect any noticeable improvement in the company's earnings," said an analyst, who declined to be named.
